overview:
For most of the fifteenth century a state centred on Cusco, in the high valleys of the southern Peruvian Andes, absorbed neighbours at a pace that has few parallels anywhere. Its people called it Tawantinsuyu, the four parts joined together — four provincial quarters radiating from the capital. By tradition the turn came in 1438, when the ruler remembered as Pachacuti beat back a Chanca attack on Cusco, took the throne, and began pushing conquests beyond the home valley; his son Topa Inca Yupanqui and grandson Huayna Capac carried the frontier thousands of kilometres further. At its greatest reach around 1500 the empire ran some 5,500 kilometres from what is now southern Colombia and Ecuador down through Peru and Bolivia into central Chile and northwest Argentina, holding on the order of two million square kilometres and somewhere between six and fourteen million subjects who spoke dozens of languages. It was, in territory, the largest state in the Americas and among the largest in the world at the time — and it was built and run without writing, without wheeled transport, and without money.

What held it together was an unusually inventive administration. Instead of taxing goods, the state taxed labour: households owed rotating service, the mit'a, on roads, terraces, mines, garrisons, and imperial estates, and were fed and supplied from state storehouses while they worked. Whole communities, mitmaqkuna, were transplanted across the empire to dilute rebellious regions or seed loyal ones. Accounts, censuses, and tribute obligations were recorded on khipu, knotted cord devices whose numerical registers scholars can read and whose possible narrative content they still argue over. More than forty thousand kilometres of engineered road, punctuated by way stations and worked by relay runners, tied the quarters to Cusco, where the sun temple of Coricancha anchored a religion of Inti and the mountain and earth powers, and where the mummified bodies of dead rulers kept their estates, their retinues, and a voice in politics. That last arrangement had a cost: each new Inca had to conquer his own wealth, which built expansion into the system.

The end came fast and from two directions at once. An epidemic, most likely smallpox travelling ahead of the Europeans themselves, appears to have killed Huayna Capac around 1528 along with his designated heir, and the empire fell into a savage succession war between his sons Huascar and Atahualpa. Atahualpa had just won it when Francisco Pizarro landed with fewer than two hundred men, and in November 1532 seized him at Cajamarca. A colossal ransom in gold and silver was paid and Atahualpa was killed anyway, in 1533; Pizarro took Cusco later that year. Andean resistance did not stop there — a rump Inca state held out in the forested country of Vilcabamba until 1572 — but the empire as a functioning whole was gone within about a year of first contact.
significance: Tawantinsuyu is the standing counterexample to the idea that large complex states require writing, currency, markets, or the wheel; it managed a continent-spanning population through reciprocal labour obligation, mass resettlement, engineered infrastructure, and cord-based record keeping, and it did so within roughly three generations. Its collapse is equally consequential: the speed with which a handful of Europeans toppled it — riding a succession war and an epidemic they did not have to start — became a template for how the Spanish empire, and later historians, explained conquest, and the silver and labour systems the colonizers grafted onto Inca institutions, above all a distorted mit'a feeding the mines of Potosí, shaped the world economy for centuries. Its roads, terraces, and stonework are still in use or still standing, and Quechua remains the most widely spoken Indigenous language in the Americas.
coverage: This dataset holds no mapped events for the story, so the overview is written entirely from reference works and secondary summaries rather than from anything the map can display. The deeper problem is the record itself: the Incas left no writing, so nearly all narrative history comes from Spanish chronicles and Andean-authored colonial texts composed decades after the conquest, by people with stakes in the outcome, and the dynastic sequence and its dates are court tradition rather than documentation. The 1438 start date in particular is a convention drawn from a 1586 chronicle; radiocarbon and Bayesian dating from Inca sites in Ecuador, Argentina, and coastal Peru now point to imperial presence in the provinces decades earlier, and the neat one-ruler-per-conquest chronology is likely a retrospective tidying. Population figures, the scale of epidemic mortality before 1532, and the readability of narrative khipu are all genuinely unsettled.
